hypothesis: If the sutural line of a turreted shell such as Turritella is a geodesic of the shell's enveloping right cone, then the number of whorls the suture makes cannot exceed the number of turns a conical geodesic can make: a geodesic on a right cone of apical angle alpha develops into a straight line on a sector of angle 2*pi*sin(alpha/2), sweeps at most pi of that sector, and therefore turns at most N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) times in total (and only half of that while approaching the apex). Measured whorl counts of Turritella shells must therefore satisfy N_obs <= N_geo.
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. From published per-specimen measurements of Turritellidae giving both the apical angle alpha and the total whorl number N_obs (Pandita et al. 2013, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6, 50 specimens of 5 species), compute N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) and the ratio R = N_obs / N_geo for every specimen with both values. SUPPORTS if at least 90% of specimens have R <= 1 (whorl count within the geodesic bound).
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. REFUTES if at least 90% of specimens have R > 1, i.e. the suture coils more times than any geodesic of the enveloping cone can, so the sutural line cannot be a conical geodesic. Between 10% and 90% is 'mixed'. If the tables cannot be retrieved or parsed, inconclusive with reason data-unavailable. The claim's first part (coils tighten toward the apex) is shared by a geodesic and by the logarithmic helico-spiral and is not discriminating; the verdict rests on the identification of the suture with a geodesic.
interpretation: Thompson's 'spiral geodetic' on a right cone is taken literally (a curve of zero geodesic curvature on the enveloping cone), and 'the sutural line ... such as Turritella ... is a geodetic of this kind' as the claim that the suture follows such a curve. The enveloping surface of a turritellid is close to a right circular cone whose apical angle is the measured alpha. The test uses only two gross measurements per shell, apical angle and whorl number, because the geodesic bound on the number of turns depends on nothing else. Whorl counts in the source include the early (protoconch/juvenile) whorls, where the cone approximation is roughest; the result is checked for sensitivity by also subtracting two whorls from every count.
